Hourly rates paid at Gillams, Bay of Islands, Newfoundland, on wharf repairs during the same period were: foreman, $2.15; carpenter, $2.00; labourer, $1.35. That answers part 2.
In answer to part 3, rates paid by the Department of Public Works on various projects across Canada are established on the basis of advice from the Department of Labour as to what rates prevail in the area concerned and at the time concerned. The explanation for the difference in this case is that Gillams is closer to Corner Brook than Cox's Cove, and many of the workers in Gillams are actually employed in Corner Brook. Therefore rates in Gillams are affected more by rates prevailing in Corner Brook. Workers at Cox's Cove are mainly involved in fishing and woods work, and the rates paid by the department there are based on rates provided by the labour department survey as prevailing in Cox's Cove and in other centres in the area.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REASSEMBLING OF SUPERVISORY
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, in view of the report that Russia has given a reply favourable to restoring the Laos international commission, I wonder if the Secretary of State for External Affairs could give us any comment as to whether this new commission is likely to be re-established.

speakeroldname: Hon. Howard C. Green (Secretary of State for External Affairs):
speakerposition: Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REASSEMBLING OF SUPERVISORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, there have been two developments of major significance in respect of Laos during the last few days. The first was that the Soviet union replied on February 18 to the proposals made by the United Kingdom about the reconvening of the international supervisory commission for Laos. These exchanges between the co-chairmen of the Geneva conference-that is the United Kingdom and the Soviet union-are,
Inquiries of the Ministry of course, confidential, and must remain so until the co-chairmen decide to make them public. I can, however, say that further discussions between the co-chairmen appear likely. Canada has, of course, a direct interest in the outcome of these discussions because, as I informed the house on January 16, we are willing, if the United Kingdom and the Soviet union as co-chairmen of the Geneva conference so request, and subject to the agreement of the king of Laos, to appoint a Canadian representative to the commission.
The second development was a declaration on February 19-one day later-by the king of Laos in which he pointed out that the policy of the royal Laotian government is one of non-alignment, non-interference and good neighbourliness; that is to say a policy of neutrality. Further, the king appealed to all countries to respect the independence, sovereignty, territorial integrity and neutrality of Laos, and to renounce all intervention in the internal affairs of the kingdom, even in the form of aid if not sanctioned by international agreements. He went on to express the hope that Cambodia, Burma and Malaya, all close neighbours would form a commission to proceed to Laos in order to establish that the country threatens no one and aspires solely to peace. The purpose of the commission would be to take action to denounce all foreign intervention, direct or indirect, which would imperil the kingdom's independence, integrity and neutrality.
I should like to remind the house that the maintenance of the sovereignty, independence, unity and integrity of Laos, and peace and stability in southeast Asia, are objectives which Canada has sought to promote for many years. In line with this policy, Canada welcomes the declaration of neutrality made by the king of Laos on behalf of his government and his people, and will continue to respect and support the independence, sovereignty and neutrality of the kingdom, as it has in the past.
With these two suggestions having been made the situation is unclear at the moment. It may be that there will have to be some joining together of the two proposals, but at the present time I am not sure just what will happen with regard to the commission in respect of Laos.

Toronto township councillors have blocked extension of a runway at Malton airport until dominion Department of Transport officials are ready to tell them how loud jet noise will be from the big expanded jetport. Mr. Speaker, I am not aware of any runway hold-up at Malton airport. As far as runway construction is concerned, we own all the land necessary for our program this year and there will not be any hold-up at this airport.

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I should like to direct a question to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources. In his absence yesterday I gave notice to the officials of his department of my intention to ask this question.
Inquiries of the Ministry
In view of the very urgent need for a policy of housing reform in the Yukon generally and in Whitehorse particularly, can the minister say whether the federal government intends to assist in any way in the immediate relief of a situation which is causing serious health and welfare problems?

speakeroldname: Hon. Walter Dinsdale (Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
subtopic: YUKON TERRITORY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I thank the hon. member for his interest in this matter, and I am happy to inform him that an urban renewal program is being developed for the city of Whitehorse to meet the problems mentioned in his question.
The federal government is prepared to lend the territory $145,000 both to purchase land for a new subdivision and to lend the city of Whitehorse funds for roads and utilities. It is estimated that over 100 families will find accommodation in this new area. We are also providing $25,000 to assist in moving to this subdivision or to other approved lots and houses which meet the area's building standards.
The federal government will also participate in a $300,000 low rental apartment project similar to urban renewal apartments in the south. This will provide at least 35 housing units. We will meet our normal 75 per cent share of the cost and are prepared also to lend the territorial government the remaining 25 per cent to encourage early development.
Finally, my department is studying details of a proposal to establish, in co-operation with the territorial government, a home building loan fund to help meet the need in the territory for funds to construct less expensive houses than those which can be approved under N.H.A. regulations. It is hoped that this study can be completed in time for the 1961 construction season in the territory.

Mr. Chairman, the caveat that I should like to register here really goes back to much more than this particular bill. It goes back to previous bills like it that have been brought in by ministers of transport. I feel that the minister did not give us enough information. I feel that ministers of transport rarely give us enough preliminary information. Then when we get into the committee examination process, in my opinion the actual statement by the officials who appear before the committee is never as satisfactory as it might be. I should like to give an indication of what dissatisfies me about this bill, although our party is anxious that it should go through.
It is necessary for me to start, Mr. Chairman, with an incident that gave me rather a shock a little bit over a year ago when we were investigating a situation concerning the province of Quebec, the city of Montreal and the federal government in relation to the Jacques Cartier bridge. We discovered the agreement that had been in effect lapsed or abrogated-I do not know what would be the technical term-for a number of years. That was one side of it. Another side was that before changes could be made in connection with the agreement, there needed to be a new table of tariffs in connection with the project; and again it appears that no really strenuous final efforts moving through to a solution had been made to bring this result about. The reason that was given to

me by the witness on the stand was that I just did not understand or appreciate the Quebec situation.
It may well be that an outsider cannot appreciate the Quebec situation and the kind of arrangement and diplomacy that needs to go on there between the federal government and the provincial government. But here we have a situation in which this government is going to spend a considerable amount of money guaranteeing a line in the province of Quebec that has more than just ordinary ramifications. It makes possible expenditures of some $50,000,000 in total if you include the refinery and the actual mine, and much more than that if you include the railway expense, the expense of building the town-site and the expense that the provincial government is going to have in putting in the road. In this kind of situation, I think we deserve more information.
At our committee meeting I was rather shocked to discover that the Minister of Transport has not had discussions with the minister who is in charge of natural resources in Quebec. I was just amazed that the minister, in connection with a project of this size, with so much government money going into it, has no idea where it is intended the refinery shall be. He just had the general expectation that it is going to be on deep water. He could give us no real information as Minister of Transport on what the factors were in the location other than the question of power and deep water. We were not given, by the company's witnesses or by the minister, any information that would indicate just where it should go.
One of the arguments I should like to make to the minister and to the committee is that we undertake big development projects of this kind on too haphazard a basis. I have here an article from the Financial Post of February 4, 1961. It is headed "Not Much Cheer for Lead, Zinc". It states as follows:
Canada's lead-zinc industry-which has hitherto sold half its output to the U.S.-gets little cheer from legislation before the House of Representatives this week.
Then it goes on to point out that there is before the U.S. house a new bill that is backed by the industry, and that has more congressional sympathy and the support of President Kennedy. What this bill sets out to do is really not to liberalize quotas but to protect the lead-zinc industry of the United States even more. The article goes on to state as follows:
What effect more protection for U.S. mines will have on Canada's three major potential producers is a question mark.
Canadian National Railways
Mattagami Lake Mines in Quebec, Brunswick Mining & Smelting in New Brunswick and Consolidated Mining & Smelting-controlled by Pine Point Mines in the Northwest Territories are planning big new mines.
Their combined, planned capacity could add more than 150,000 tons of lead and more than 400,000 tons of zinc to Canada's annual production-double present output.
In other words, we have on the cards- and this mine is a factor-a doubling of our zinc production in this country. Yet ever since I came into this House of Commons, the then hon. member for Kootenay East not the present hon. member, used to be always getting to his feet and worrying about the difficulties that Consolidated Mining and Smelting were having in getting rid of this production in the United States' market and in the world market. My particular point here is that there are indications that on the short run the zinc prospects are not good. Yet we are to have a doubling of capacity. When you have a situation like this it seems to me that we should know more about the kind of agreement that a crown corporation is entering into with the particular mining concern. There is nothing statutory about this agreement. I know it has a legal status, but not for members of parliament. In essence it is outside us in that it does not come within the act that is before us. Another feature about this question of the agreement is this: We had some evidence last year brought out by the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, the hon. member for Laurier and myself in the questioning of the president of the Canadian National Railways about the various development lines that he had investigated. He indicated some of the principles that are involved as far as the Canadian National Railways are concerned in setting up these lines. At page 142 of the minutes of proceedings and evidence of the sessional committee on railways, air lines and shipping he stated as follows:
The Canadian National Railways was the originator of this traffic guarantee form of approach to this problem, and we originated it because of past experience where railway lines were pushed, back in the days when political considerations had something to do with these matters-happily gone now The railways were pushed on that basis, whether it was completely economical for the railway to build the line or not. So we do it on an arm's length basis and consider all the interests not only of the industry that wants the service but also the general effect to the community; and on the basis of our appraisal we are prepared to take care of our share of the risk.
It seems to me we have to take from this statement of policy of the president that they have gone into this whole matter. However, I would argue that we did not get satisfactory answers on this question from the officials of the railway who were before us. I refer to the general effect on the community. What
2314	HOUSE OF
Canadian National Railways do we know about this matter? It is surely an integrated operation. What do we know about the general effect to the community? We do not know where the refinery is going to be. We do not know whether all the productions from the mine, in terms of concentrates, is going to be shipped all the way to the refinery by the Canadian National Railway. We do not know what are the views of the provincial government of Quebec in the matter.
It seems to me these are all matters about which we could have more information. My own views and the good judgment of the Canadian National Railways executive are not particularly sanguine. I hope to express them later this day when we are considering the motion to set up a committee. But it seems to me, when we have a crown corporation that year after year has been burying itself further and further in deficits, and when we have indications even from Mr. Gordon's own analysis last year of these branch lines that at times traffic has not been everything that could be expected, it all adds up to the fact that we deserve and should have more detail on the agreement and on the project in total, where it is going to go and what it is going to do.
In conclusion of my comments on this matter, may I say I have often wondered what approach the minister takes when he is shepherding a bill through the house. It seems to me that the minister gives the members of the house the fairest treatment when he decides that through his preliminary statement he is going to cover every possible aspect of the situation. Then we have something on the record. I suggest to the present minister that he gives every indication of someone who is going to be very chary in the amount of information he provides.
I am not giving him advice; I am asking him in future, when he is bringing a bill before the house even though it is later going to committee, to cover all the ramifications of the matter. I think he would then save a great deal of the questioning that we have in committee, which often turns out to be futile, and many of the complaints that we have later.
Specifically I should like to know from the minister what attention the government is paying to the views of the people in the Abitibi country that they would like to have a refinery up there. I know this is a legitimate point of view because the people in my part of the country are very anxious to have a smelter, for example, at the lakehead to process the ores that are very close to us.
This is the kind of thing that keens and burns people in an area for many, many years. They ask, "Why was a refinery or a


smelter not established in our particular area, instead of being way up somewhere else?" I know the answer the minister gave about the economics of the situation, but the people in the region have a hard time believing some of these particular economics and I am sure they wonder why governments do not get together and try to direct a refinery or a smelter in such a way, even if necessary by subsidization, as to be an integrated part of the economy in the area.
If the minister says this is an interference with free enterprise, I suggest the subsidization of this refinery is an interference with free enterprise. Once you are in the situation of guaranteeing a crown corporation going into the area to help exploit private enterprise, surely you are in a position to suggest to that private enterprise that it do its utmost to help the particular region and economy that it is developing.
The other point I should like to make in connection with this whole arrangement is sparked a bit by the minister but also by the hon. member for Villeneuve. I think I made the same error myself. We talk grandiosely about our tremendous natural resources. One of the things mentioned is that this railway line is going to open up a tremendous pulp and paper area. We have more potential pulp scattered around this country that is not being exploited than we know what to do with. We always live in dreams. I come from a town that since 1922 has been told by politician after politician that some day there is going to be a large pulp mill there. I know the sense of disappointment people feel. All through northern Quebec, if my reading is correct-and my reading is necessarily skimpy-there are hopes that pulp and paper mills will be constructed. In a situation such as this, I think the minister should have more information on what is the potential cordage. What is this government itself doing to see that if we put in a railway line there is going to be some industrial development such as a pulp mill, whether it is newsprint, kraft or whatever the case may be? It seems to me these are all the kind of questions associated with resource development that should be answered in this house and in the committees of the house.
In summing it up, it is a case where we do a tremendous lot of dreaming and big talk about our resources, and then on something like this we vote the money very readily. I think it is a tremendous thing that we are going to have a line of this scope and size. However, there are some doubtful factors in it and we are not given the complete complex of the situation. Unless governments in Canada, and the federal government in particular, are prepared to take the kind of

initiative that will develop the thing wholly in the best interests of all, I think we are going to have this damnable failure of government enterprise and free enterprise working together and neither one really giving the leadership that is needed to develop our hinterland and frontier resources.
I think the most wonderful thing that could happen to the Abitibi region of Quebec would be to get not only the mine but also the refinery. I hesitate to accept the argument that a tidewater or a deep water location is fundamental in the economics. I should like to know what are the economics, and perhaps the government of Quebec could do something about shifting them so that the refinery would be placed where it would really do the most good.
I should like to ask the minister one specific question. Has the location or the development of this Brunswick Mining and Smelting property in New Brunswick anything to do with the location of the refinery? That is, are the concentrates from it expected to be treated at this particular refinery that may be going to deep water? That may go some way to explaining the location down on the St. Lawrence rather than in the Abitibi area itself.
In relation to the Abitibi region itself, any hinterland or frontierland area is always told it really has not a large enough labour market to support a complex industry such as a refinery. There are a number of members in this house who come from hinterland and frontier regions and I think they will tell you that labour mobility today is high enough that you do not have to worry about the labour market and the high cost of labour in the those regions. You can be sure that if in Canada there is going to be a new town of a continuing size and a good opportunity to make a go, you will get a flood of people coming into it. This happened at Elliott Lake with very stark results. That is an indication that you can get people to move very easily from metropolitan areas if they know there is a guarantee of remunerative work with some stability.
This is my final point in suggesting that we are entitled to have a certain disappointment about the way this particular bill has been introduced and taken through to this stage.

I have a remark to make with regard to the schedule, Mr. Chairman. Could the minister tell us if there is a marked difference between the estimated cost of the Canadian National and the actual cost?
Of course, he would be unable to answer that question with regard to the present line, because it has not yet been built.
However, the transport division must have faced that situation on some previous occasion. I cannot remember it right now, but, was the estimated cost of the Canadian National in the past not exceeded by the actual cost?

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
My hon. friend asked that question in the committee on railways, canals and telegraph lines, the other day, and I have made some inquiries since.
With regard to the Beattyville-Chibouga-mau-St. Felicien line, which was, I think, built in 1954, the estimate for the 294 miles of track was $35 million, which meant an average cost per mile of $119,184,
The expenses actually incurred amounted to $34,788,219, or an average cost of $118,126 per mile.
We realize therefore that the margin between expenses and estimates was very slight. Nowadays, building costs are higher. That is why the basic estimate of $119,000, made in 1954, when the Beattyville-Chibou-gamau-St. Felicien line was built, has now increased to $140,000 for the same distance, that is, one mile.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext: It is obvious that formerly, the actual cost exceeded the cost estimated by the Canadian National Railways and I suppose we may safely conclude that it will be again the case for the construction of this line.

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
When I looked over the
statistics for the last ten years, year by year, I realized that the estimated cost always went up, which means that it was regularly higher than for the preceding period.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
The building costs may, of course, increase, but that is not my point.
What I would like to know is this: Considering past experience, and also the known figures, can the estimate of the Canadian National Railways which now amounts to $140,000 per mile, be exceeded once the railway line is built, let us say in 1962?

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext: No. I do not quite get the question. The hon. member asks whether the estimated cost arrived at by the C.N.R. or rather whether the C.N.R. will have to prepare new estimates as the months go by. Well, it will not be so. Since the amount is set for the whole contract, the amount will not be greater for the last month than for the first months of the contract.

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext: It is hypothetical question.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext:
Perhaps my question was not quite clear, but it was surely not hypothetical as the hon. member for Charlevoix (Mr. Asselin) seems to suggest.
The figures given by the minister indicate that the estimated cost of the C.N.R. with regard to the railway lines that have been built, those from Chibougamau to St. Felicien, from Beattyville to Chibougamau, and from Barraute to Kiask Falls, has been exceeded in each case. It is a fact.
I am not referring to the increase of construction cost. That is a quite different matter. My point is that the C.N.R. said, according to its estimate-and I refer to the cost per mile only-that it would be $140,000 a mile. Now, I ask whether, in view of the experience with the Canadian National, you think that the $140,000 estimate will be exceeded once the line is completed.

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE

tion on normal cost figures for that kind of project. Anyway, it is not up to me, as a mere layman, to say whether the $140,000 figure is or is not a good estimate.

speakerposition: Official Opposition House Leader; Liberal Party House Leader
subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE
speechtext: Now, on January 16 the minister tabled in this house document number 149 which fully explains the expenditures on the building of three railways, those from St. Felicien to Lac Cache, from Beattyville to Lac Cache, and from Hillsport to Mani-towadge Lake. Could the minister tell us what percentage of this sum, for instance, would have been spent for land expropriation, engineering work, clearing, grading, bridge building, telephone and telegraph lines, stations, etc? Have the C.N.R. officials prepared a similar statement to that which was tabled in the house?

I cannot understand why the member for Laurier did not ask his questions at that time. I am certainly not in a position to give him any figures. He asked for certain technical details, strictly pertaining to civil engineering, and technical details about building, and I cannot give them to him. If he had advised me of his intention two or three days ago, I could have done so. But, now-
I sincerely wonder why he insists and why he did not seek that information when the C.N.R. experts were available to the committee.

subtopic: AUTHORITY FOR CONSTRUCTION OF BRANCH LINE

Well, Mr. Chairman, I have asked the committee several questions, and I have received some information. On other points, I did not get the answer I was seeking. But that is not the point. Now, we are no longer in the railway committee but in committee of the whole, and it is the minister's responsibility to supply the required information.
The minister can certainly not say that I took advantage of him today. I asked him some questions which seemed simple to me.
I asked questions that came to my mind without having prepared them beforehand.
Canadian National Railways I have here the document which the minister tabled himself in this house, and he seemed surprised when I asked him how the nine and odd million dollars provided for that line would be distributed in respect of expropriation, engineering work, and so on. That was certainly not a question which should surprise him, as it was based on a document which he tabled in the house which he has seen and probably studied. I am asking a quite natural question.
